candidates.title: "MAID (Mobility Aid Image Dataset): An Annotated Image Dataset for Recognizing Wheelchair Types for Accessible Curbside Transport"
candidates.description: "Accessible vehicles must prepare differently for a manual and a powered wheelchair: ramp or lift, interior space, and securement all depend on the device. Camera-based perception could tell a vehicle which type is approaching, but widely used vision datasets either have no wheelchair class or a single one, insufficient for accessible mobility solutions, especially towards autonomous vehicles as assistive robotics for transit. Our contribution, MAID, is a face-blurred image dataset of 455 open-licensed photographs labeled for device type (manual, powered, other mobility aid, and ambiguous wheelchair-like objects such as off-road tricycles. occupancy, attendant presence, occlusion, viewpoint, lighting, and setting. 6 of these 455 were labeled unclear on device type, so we split only the other 449 images with a determinable type 70\/15\/15 into train, validation, and test sets that keep duplicates, uploaders, creators, and photo series within one split. The 6 images labeled unclear are released separately from the main 449 in an excluded folder. Our labels only describe the device and the scene, and never attempt to label a person\u2019s identity, age, diagnosis, or disability. We release a data dictionary, per-image license and attribution records, along with six baselines as evidence of application. The best model on validation, SigLIP 2 with its last four blocks fine-tuned, reaches 0.90 accuracy and 0.84 macro-F1 on the 64-image test set. However, SigLIP-based performance estimates may be optimistic because annotators were exposed to model-generated label suggestions."

candidates.title: AI Regulation Media Texts Dataset: Comparable Corpora in Czech and Portuguese (2018-2023)
candidates.description: AI Regulation Media Texts Dataset: Comparable Corpora in Czech and Portuguese (2018-2023) is a collection of online mainstream news articles on Artificial Intelligence (AI) regulation in the European Union context. It consists of texts between 2018 and 2023, focusing on Czech and Portuguese media outlets. For analytical purposes, the dataset comprises two comparable textual corpora (texts on a given topic, from a given period, and representing a specific part of the media sector), one for each country in the given language. The dataset was collected as part of the project CORRELATE – Corpora and Lexical and Terminological Resources ( https://clunl.fcsh.unl.pt/en/projetos/projetos-curso/correlate-corpora-e-recursos-lexicais-e-terminologicos/ ). The data was collected through a combination of downloading from the paid media database Annopress (Czech corpus) and web scraping, using BootCat 1.57 (Portuguese corpus). Considering this, the data is available solely for further academic and scientific use (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). The search was based on the common seed terms related to “artificial intelligence” and “EU regulation”, or the specific title of the EU’s “AI Act” document, including synonyms and different clusters, in each language. Specific mainstream online media outlets were selected, as classified by NFNZ and Netmonitor for Czechia (22 media outlets) and by Netaudience and Clube de Imprensa for Portugal (32 media outlets), and published between March 2018 and December 2023. This period is defined by the establishment of the first AI expert group and the European AI alliance in 2018, and the final political agreement on the “AI Act” regulation in 2023. The Czech corpus consists of 659,388 tokens, distributed across 675 articles, from March 2018 until December 2023. The Portuguese corpus covers the same time periods and comprises 539,199 tokens, distributed across 361 articles. The corpora were cleaned of duplicates (based on URL, text content, and title) and shallow-processed (tokenisation, lemmatisation, and POS tagging) using Sketch Engine software. Enabling more nuanced analysis, the corpora also include the following metadata: source/medium, author, publication year, URL. Both resulting corpora are available in two formats: plain text (.txt) and shallow-processed vertical file or word-per-line format (.vert), useful for further linguistic corpus analysis. candidates.title: Dataset for: Vibrometry as a noncontact alternative to dynamic and viscoelastic mechanical testing in cartilage
candidates.description: Physiological loading of knee cartilage is highly dynamic and may contribute to the progression of osteoarthritis. Thus, an understanding of cartilage’s dynamic mechanical properties is crucial in cartilage research. In this study, vibrometry was used as a fast (2 hours), noncontact, and novel alternative to the slower (30 hours), traditional mechanical and biochemical assays for characterization of cartilage from the condyle, patella, trochlear groove, and meniscus. Finite-element models predicted tissue resonant frequencies and bending modes, which strongly correlated with experiments (R 2 =0.93). Vibrometry-based viscoelastic properties significantly correlated with moduli from stress relaxation and creep tests, with correlation strengths reaching up to 0.78. Loss modulus also strongly correlated with GAG content. Dynamic properties measured by vibrometry significantly differed among various knee cartilages, ranging between 6.1-56.4MPa. Interestingly, meniscus viscoelastic properties suggest that contrary to common belief, it may lack shock absorption abilities; instead, condylar hyaline cartilage may be a better shock absorber. These data demonstrate for the first time that vibrometry is a noncontact approach to dynamic mechanical characterization of hyaline and fibrocartilage cartilage with concrete relationships to standard quasistatic mechanical testing and biochemical composition. Thus, with a single tool, vibrometry greatly facilitates meeting multiple regulatory recommendations for mechanical characterization of cartilage replacements.

candidates.title: ME-AD: Progressive Robotics Anomaly Detection Dataset
candidates.description: Introduction The ME-AD (Mitsubishi Electric Anomaly Detection) dataset contains operating data of cyclic pick-and-place executions collected from a 6-DoF Mitsubishi Electric RV-7FM-D1-S15 manipulator under progressive actuation degradation. A defect was intentionally introduced in the actuator of joint 3 (removal of gearbox lubricant), causing gradual mechanical wear over pick-and-place cycles. Unlike existing robotics AD datasets where anomalies are artificially induced, ME-AD documents an actual progressive hardware fault, making it uniquely suited for benchmarking semi-supervised anomaly detection, online/early fault detection, and remaining useful life estimation. At a Glance The size of the unzipped dataset is ~10GB. The dataset contains approximately 17,000 pick-and-place cycles organized into 7 operation groups called tasks across 3 motion families. Each cycle includes joint positions, velocities, accelerations, and torques sampled at ~280 Hz. The dataset provides raw CSV files, cleaned Pandas DataFrames (.pkl), and pre-configured AD task splits. Each data sample contains 6 joint positions (rad), 6 joint velocities (rad/s), 6 joint accelerations (rad/s²), and 6 joint torques (Nm). Processed files include both raw and low-pass filtered signals. ME-AD/ contains: CSV/ (raw per-cycle CSV files organized by operation code), Pandas/ (cleaned .pkl DataFrames per cycle), Tasks/ (7 pre-configured AD benchmark tasks with training/healthy/faulty splits), and Python scripts for data processing and task generation. The README.md file contains further details. CarHoods10k thus enables the evaluate of data-driven approaches for application in the automotive engineering design domain and others.

candidates.title: SNP dataset for cape race brook trout
candidates.description: Many studies have investigated the loss of adaptive potential in endangered or exploited species experiencing recent population declines. Less research has studied adaptive genomic variation in small populations known to have persisted for long periods, despite the unique contribution that such populations provide for determining mechanisms underlying population persistence in evolutionary and conservation modeling. Small populations of Brook trout ( Salvelinus fontinalis ) have persisted in Cape Race, Newfoundland for >12,000 years. We used genotyping-by-sequencing data to investigate the demographic history and adaptive genomic variation of 26 populations with effective population sizes (N e ) ranging from 11 to 442, and to explore mechanisms underlying long-term persistence. We show that all populations experienced demographic declines following postglacial colonization but have remained in their current, small N e state for thousands of years. We also reveal greater homozygosity in adaptive alleles within the smallest populations and found signatures of adaptive divergence in small populations relating to several abiotic and biotic factors. Our study illustrates how the demographic history of a species can influence the adaptive dynamics of small populations persisting over long time periods.

candidates.title: [ITU AI/ML Challenge 2021] Dataset IEEE 802.11ax Spatial Reuse
candidates.description: This dataset has been created for the problem statement ITU-ML5G-PS-004 of the ITU AI/ML Challenge (2021 edition). More information can be found here: https://challenge.aiforgood.itu.int/ and https://www.upf.edu/web/wnrg/2021-edition . The dataset contains the information of 3.000 IEEE 802.11ax deployments (divided into two different scenarios) at which the Basic Service Set (BSS) of interest applies different possible OBSS/PD thresholds in the context of the Spatial Reuse (SR) operation. In total, 21 OBSS/PD values are considered for each deployment, and some of the deployments include data from different STA locations. The provided files are expected to be used for training Machine Learning (ML) and Federated Learning (FL) algorithms. More specifically, the dataset is divided as follows: Scenario 1: 1,000 different deployments with 2-6 APs and 1 STA per AP. A minimum distance limitation is applied, so that each AP different from AP_A is located at a minimum distance of 10 meters from that one. Each deployment is simulated for each of the 21 possible OBSS/PD thresholds in 11ax. Two files are considered: output_11ax_sr_simulations_sce1.txt : contains the output generated by the simulator for the deployments in Scenario 1. simulator_input_files_sce1.zip : contains the input files used by the simulator to simulate the deployments in Scenario 1. Scenario 2: 1,000 different deployments with 2-6 APs and 1-4 STAs per AP. No distance limitation is applied. Each deployment is simulated for each of the 21 possible OBSS/PD thresholds in 11ax. Two files are considered: output_11ax_sr_simulations_sce2.txt : contains the output generated by the simulator for the deployments in Scenario 2. simulator_input_files_sce2.zip : contains the input files used by the simulator to simulate the deployments in Scenario 2. Scenario 3: 1,000 different deployments with 2-6 APs and 1-4 STAs per AP. No distance limitation is applied. Each deployment is simulated for each of the 21 possible OBSS/PD thresholds in 11ax, and for up to 20 different locations of different STAs of the BSS of interest ("BSS_A"). Two files are considered: output_11ax_sr_simulations_sce3.txt : contains the output generated by the simulator for the deployments in Scenario 3. simulator_input_files_sce3.zip : contains the input files used by the simulator to simulate the deployments in Scenario 3. Test: 1,000 different deployments with 2-6 APs and 1-4 STAs per AP. No distance limitation is applied. A random OBSS/PD threshold is applied. Two files are considered: output_11ax_sr_simulations_test.txt : contains the output generated by the simulator for the evaluation deployments. The label (throughput) has been replaced with "0s". simulator_input_files_test.zip : contains the input files used by the simulator to simulate the evaluation deployments.

candidates.description: Myoelectric control has emerged as a promising approach for a wide range of applications, including controlling limb prosthetics, teleoperating robots, and enabling immersive interactions in the metaverse. The latter has received less attention despite its significant impact on signal quality and decoding accuracy. To address this gap, we present GREAT, a novel dataset of surface electromyographic (EMG) signals captured from multiple arm positions. This dataset, comprising EMG and hand kinematics data from 8 participants performing 6 different hand gestures, provides a comprehensive resource for investigating position-invariant myoelectric control decoding algorithms. We envision this dataset to serve as a valuable resource for both training and benchmarking arm position-invariant myoelectric control algorithms. Additionally, to further expand the publicly available data capturing the variability of EMG signals across diverse arm positions, we propose a novel data acquisition protocol that can be utilized for future data collection.

candidates.title: Robotic manipulation datasets for offline compositional reinforcement learning
candidates.description: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising direction that allows RL agents to be pre-trained from large datasets avoiding recurrence of expensive data collection. To advance the field, it is crucial to generate large-scale datasets. Compositional RL is particularly appealing for generating such large datasets, since 1) it permits creating many tasks from few components, and 2) the task structure may enable trained agents to solve new tasks by combining relevant learned components. This submission provides four offline RL datasets for simulated robotic manipulation created using the 256 tasks from CompoSuite [Mendez et al., 2022] ( https://github.com/Lifelong-ML/CompoSuite ). In every task in CompoSuite, a *robot* arm is used to manipulate an *object* to achieve an *objective* all while trying to avoid an *obstacle*. There are for components for each of these four axes that can be combined arbitrarily leading to a total of 256 tasks. The component choices are * Robot: IIWA, Jaco, Kinova3, Panda * Object: Hollow box, box, dumbbell, plate * Objective: Push, pick and place, put in shelf, put in trashcan * Obstacle: None, wall between robot and object, wall between goal and object, door between goal and object The four included datasets are collected using separate agents each trained to a different degree of performance, and each dataset consists of 256 million transitions. The degrees of performance are expert data, medium data, warmstart data and replay data: * Expert dataset: Transitions from an expert agent that was trained to achieve 90% success on every task. * Medium dataset: Transitions from a medium agent that was trained to achieve 30% success on every task. * Warmstart dataset: Transitions from a Soft-actor critic agent trained for a fixed duration of one million steps. * Medium-replay-subsampled dataset: Transitions that were stored during the training of a medium agent up to 30% success. These datasets are intended for the combined study of compositional generalization and offline reinforcement learning.

candidates.title: A high-resolution and whole-body dataset of hand-object contact areas based on 3D scanning method
candidates.description: Hand contact data, reflecting the intricate behaviours of human hands during object operation, exhibits significant potential for analysing hand operation patterns to guide the design of hand-related sensors and robots, and predicting object properties. However, these potential applications are hindered by the constraints of low resolution and incomplete capture of the hand contact data. Leveraging a non-contact and high-precision 3D scanning method for surface capture, a high-resolution and whole-body hand contact dataset, named as Ti3D-contact, is constructed in this work. The dataset, with an average resolution of 0.72 mm, contains 1872 sets of texture images and 3D models. The contact area during hand operation is whole-body painted on gloves, which are captured as the high-resolution original hand contact data through a 3D scanner. Reliability validation on Ti3D-contact is conducted and hand movement classification with 95% precision is achieved using the acquired hand contact dataset. The properties of high-resolution and whole-body capturing make the acquired dataset exhibit a promising potential application in hand posture recognition and hand movement prediction.

candidates.title: COMSOL simulation & example datasets for: Nonuniform structural properties of wings confer sensing advantages
candidates.description: Sensory feedback is essential to both animals and robotic systems for achieving coordinated, precise movements. Mechanosensory feedback, which provides information about body deformation, depends not only on the properties of sensors but also on the structure in which they are embedded. In insects, wing structure plays a particularly important role in flapping flight: in addition to generating aerodynamic forces, wings provide mechanosensory feedback necessary for guiding flight while undergoing dramatic deformations during each wingbeat. However, the role that wing structure plays in determining mechanosensory information is relatively unexplored. Insect wings exhibit characteristic stiffness gradients and are subject to both aerodynamic and structural damping. Here we examine how both of these properties impact sensory performance, using finite element analysis combined with sensor placement optimization approaches. We show that wings with nonuniform stiffness exhibit several advantages over uniform stiffness wings, resulting in higher accuracy of rotation detection and lower sensitivity to the placement of sensors on the wing. Moreover, we show that higher damping generally improves the accuracy with which body rotations can be detected. These results contribute to our understanding of the evolution of the nonuniform stiffness patterns in insect wings, as well as suggest design principles for robotic systems.

candidates.title: Dataset for: Phosphorus mobilization from intact soil monoliths flooded under simulated summer versus spring snowmelt with intermittent freeze-thaw conditions
candidates.description: Enhanced phosphorus (P) release from flooded, anaerobic soils have been extensively studied under summer temperatures, but not under cold temperatures with intermittent freeze-thaw events. We investigated the temperature and freeze/ thaw effects during flooding on the release of P to floodwater from soil monoliths (15-cm depth) collected from eight agricultural fields in Manitoba. Soil monoliths were flooded with reverse osmosis water and incubated for 56 d under simulated summer flooding (SSF, 22±1 ℃), or snowmelt flooding with intermittent freeze thaw (IFT, 4±1 ℃ with intermittent freezing) in triplicates. Redox potential (Eh), pore water and floodwater dissolved reactive P (DRP) concentrations, pH and concentrations of Ca, Mg, Fe and Mn were determined weekly. In seven soils, Eh decreased rapidly with days after flooding (DAF) under SSF to values < 200 mV, but not under IFT. Pore water and floodwater DRP concentrations significantly increased with DAF in all soils under SSF, and in seven soils under IFT. While DRP concentrations were consistently greater under SSF than IFT in four soils, other soils had similar concentrations at certain DAFs. Significant relationships between ion concentrations and redox status , that fitted both IFT and SSF data in most soils, suggests that similar redox-driven mechanisms are responsible for the P release; however, less P is released under IFT than SSF, since soils were not severely reduced under IFT. Substantial P release in a few soils under IFT, appeared to be unrelated to redox status, suggesting other P release mechanisms that are not redox driven.

candidates.title: ChildSafeLLM: A Dataset of Child Safety Aligned Evaluation Prompts for Generative AIs
candidates.description: ChildSafeLLM (Child Safety Aligned Evaluation Prompts for Generative AIs) is a developmental benchmark comprising 200 total prompts carefully crafted and curated for two distinct age cohorts—ages 6-12 and ages 7-13. Drawing on evidence-based child-safety guidelines, school curricula, and authentic questions from children and caregivers, the prompts were sourced from reputable organizations across six continents to ensure broad cultural and linguistic representation. Available in .xlsx, ChildSafeLLM supports a wide range of natural-language processing tasks, including harmful-content detection, age-appropriateness classification, response-consistency analysis, safety-alignment fine-tuning, and developmental language modeling. Beyond its use for model training, the corpus offers a reproducible benchmark for evaluating ambiguity resolution, risk-category labeling, and multi-turn dialogue safety in child–AI interactions. By standardizing safety scenarios for younger users, ChildSafeLLM advances research into trustworthy AI design and helps practitioners assess how generative models accommodate children’s cognitive and emotional needs. candidates.title: Last Interglacial sea-level data points from Northwest Europe
candidates.description: This dataset contains known preserved Last Interglacial (Eemian, Ipswichian, MIS 5e, MIS 5) sea level proxies for NW Europe: from along the shores of the English Channel and North Sea, and from their offshore areas. This V2 version includes 146 sea-level indicator data points from in and around the North Sea (35 entries in Netherlands, 10 Belgium, 23 in Germany, 17 in Denmark, 9 in Britain) and the English Channel (24 entries for the British and 25 for the French side, 3 on the Channel Isles), believed to be a representative and fairly complete inventory and assessment coming from some 80 published sites. The database also includes a modest subselection of data points from older interglacials (six sites), for comparative use. The dataset has been constructed in and has been exported from the World Atlas of Last Interglacial Shorelines (WALIS) database ( https://warmcoasts.eu/world-atlas.html ). The sea level proxies in majority are obtained from localities with well developed lithostratigraphic (MIS-6 aged ‘Saalian’ glaciogenic landforms and deposits as the substrate), morphostratigraphic (position in terrace flights), Amino-Acid Racemization, and biostratigraphic constraints ('Lusitanian' molluscan, foraminifera, pollen successions, other). The majority of European continental sites have chronostratigraphic age-control (regional encoding scheme included in dataset) notably by correlation to regional Pollen Association Zones with varve-count based durations (reckoned to span at least 11,000 years of temperate interglacial conditions; matching a good part of MIS 5e), and/or Foraminiferal Association Zones (echoing marine environmental and paleogeographic changes), and/or from AAR zones (majority of British sites, selected sites of mainland NW Europe; albeit for many sites older, lesser quality applications of the technique). In all regions, some of the marine deposits and bracketing terrestrial ones have also been independently dated using luminescence (IRSL, OSL, TL), U-series and ESR techniques.

candidates.title: Mechanical Systems of Upper Paleolithic Venery: Reinterpreting the Ithyphallic Figure and Quadrilateral Signs of Lascaux, Niaux, and Altamira as Engineered Traps
candidates.description: The parietal art of Lascaux, Niaux, and Altamira caves has long been evaluated through symbolic, mythological, or shamanistic frameworks, traditionally classifying non-figurative geometric markings as "clannish tokens" or abstract language signs. This paper presents a fundamental, empirical reinterpretation of these configurations, revealing a systemic and technically precise record of advanced mechanical hunting technology. By conducting a comparative morphological analysis using physical, full-scale timber trap reconstructions, we establish functional cross-parity with several primary configurations: the bird-headed ithyphallic figure in the Lascaux Shaft scene, the widespread "quadrilateral signs" throughout the Axial Gallery, the claviform and trigger matrices of Niaux, and the friction-based trigger vectors on the Polychrome Ceiling of Altamira. We demonstrate that the rigid, geometric stick figure is not a human representation, but a mechanical blueprint of a spring-loaded lever arm featuring a 90-degree catching-pin trigger and a vertical prop-stabilizer. Furthermore, we reveal that the quadrilateral grids represent gravity-drop deadfalls and corral systems equipped with overhead directional funnel-fences designed to guide megafauna vectors into reinforced containment fields. This evidence indicates a sophisticated mastery of kinetic energy storage, mechanical triggers, and path channelization in the Solutrean and Magdalenian periods, fundamentally shifting our understanding of Upper Paleolithic hunting behavior and cognitive mechanics. Introduction: The Upper Paleolithic cave systems of Western Europe are celebrated for their highly dynamic, anatomically accurate depictions of Pleistocene fauna. Yet, interspersed among these organic animal vectors is an expansive corpus of rigid, non-figurative lineations. For nearly a century, institutional prehistorians have relegated these markings to secondary status, categorizing them as abstract tokens or stylistic palimpsests. This study challenges the dominant symbolic paradigm, demonstrating through experimental archaeology models that these linear systems illustrate functional, highly calculated mechanical trapping architectures across multiple major geographical sites. Methodology & Experimental Design Dataset: To empirically validate the trap hypothesis, a dual-methodological framework was deployed. First, digital vector mapping was applied to the digital archives of the Lascaux Shaft scene, the quadrilateral panels of the Axial Gallery, the Salon Noir of Niaux, and the Polychrome Ceiling of Altamira to calculate explicit structural vectors, post-spacing intervals, and trigger junctions. Second, a series of period-accurate, full-scale primitive wilderness traps—specifically spring-loaded spear frames and gravity-drop deadfall cages—were physically constructed using wood, cordage, and stone tools. Lithic Tool Replication and Wood Processing: Replicated Solutrean bifacial hand-axes and unifacial chopping tools knapped from native Onondaga chert were utilized to fell primary structural poles. Bark removal and trigger-notch carving were executed exclusively using raw burins and backed blades to replicate Upper Paleolithic tool wear-patterns. Material Matrix Specifications: Primary spring-lever arms were constructed from green Betula pendula (Silver Birch) and Pinus sylvestris (Scots Pine) with diameters ranging from 4.5 cm to 7.0 cm at the base. Rigid framing and stake enclosures were sourced from seasoned Quercus robur (Oak). Bindings consisted of hand-braided, multi-ply animal sinew (deer hide) yielding a mean tensile failure threshold of 2.4 kN. Mechanical Component Metric Log:• Model A (Spring-Spear): Length 220 cm; Base Diameter 6.2 cm; 35° deflection angle under structural tension load. Perpendicular Catch-Pin: Length 12.5 cm; 90° trigger angle relative to vertical anchor stake axis. Vertical Prop-Stick: Length 85 cm.• Model B (Drop-Deadfall): Gravity Gate Mesh Width 150 cm, Height 120 cm. Directional Funnel Fences: Length 350 cm per wing at a 45° flaring vector angle. Basal Trip-Stick Trigger: Length 110 cm; 12 cm clearance above grade. Kinetic Testing and Data Acquisition: Mechanical displacement tests confirmed that Model A stored a mean potential energy capacity of 340 Joules when cocked at full draw against the 90-degree catch-pin trigger. High-speed visual data tracking verified that the trigger mechanism achieved complete structural release within 42 milliseconds of trigger-wire impact. Model B delivered a mean vertical kinetic impact force of 1.85 kN upon trigger release. Regional Technological Evaluation of the Cave Corpus: The Lascaux Shaft Scene Trigger Dynamics: The bird-headed human figure displays a rigid vector alignment completely distinct from the organic contours of the adjacent bison. The torso operates structurally as a primary spring-lever arm. The unique 90-degree perpendicular protrusion acts perfectly as a mechanical locking tooth or catch-pin designed to hold high-tensile string cordage under tension. The adjacent vertical bird-staff maps out a classic stabilization prop-stick, engineered to drop instantly upon physical game impact. The quadrilateral grids floating near the "Falling Horse" panel mirror the physical grid spacing of a gravity-drop cage. The Niaux Claviform and Trigger Matrices: In the Salon Noir, prominent linear configurations running across the flanks of the equine and bison panels terminate in a sharp, distinct inverted-V or looping notch at the rib plane. This acts as a tension-wire balance beam matching a tension release catch-pin. Rhythmic inverted chevrons and vertical hash grids correspond to a spring-loaded strike array or deadfall drop-spear frame. Pectiform signs illustrate a reinforced stake barrier or corral fence layout with teeth angled to resist outward lateral force. The Altamira Hinge and Core Balance Vectors: On the Polychrome Ceiling, distinct linear lineations intersect behind the shoulder of the primary red bison, looping out into a clear V-shape friction trigger pin setup. This line maps a high-tensile cordage line running from an anchoring stake, held in place by the trigger pin until physical movement dislodges it. Heavy vertical painted vectors cutting into the natural ceiling fissures represent structural anchoring stakes wedged into rock crevices to absorb the potential energy stored in a spring-arm sapling before it is tripped. Discussion: The systematic distribution of these functional engineering blueprints across multiple, distinct cave complexes proves that these drawings were not arbitrary tokens or passive symbols. The absolute structural symmetry between your physical wood constructions and the Upper Paleolithic lineations demonstrates that early humans possessed a sophisticated understanding of physics, structural load distribution, and kinetic release loops. By shifting our perspective back toward an empirical, mechanical functionalism, this discovery establishes the master artists of the Upper Paleolithic as the world's early industrial draftspersons.

candidates.title: Dataset of Kannada Films Produced between 1934-2022
candidates.description: Since its inception in 1934, Kannada film industry has produced more than 4000 films as of November 2022. At present, it produces an average of 90 - 100 films per year, including original productions, remakes, and adaptations. A list of Kannada films produced between 1934 and 2022 has been compiled by drawing on digital archives, online encyclopedias, blogs, and websites. To date, no comprehensive database has brought together key information about Kannada films, including, year of release director(s) production houses distributors filmic category (whether it is an originally made film or a remake or an adaptation) status re-production of films in the same or different languages source of a film in case it is a remake or an adaptation title of the source (be it a film or a literary work) year of its release or publication names of directors or writers; and the language in which it is made or written. This information was available, in fragments, on platforms such as indiancine.ma , IMDb, Wikipedia, and Kannada Movies Info, but was often incomplete, outdated, and inconsistent. These limitations made existing digital databases unreliable for sustained research. Therefore, there was a need for a reliable, consistent, and comprehensive database, and the present list of films attempts to address that need. Further, the data is of greater use for researchers in translation studies, film studies, linguistic anthropology, history, and media and communication.

candidates.title: STORM-AI: AI Challenge for Satellite Tracking and Orbit Resilience Modeling dataset
candidates.description: Precise thermospheric density forecasting is critical for mitigating satellite drag in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), but traditional empirical models such as MSIS and JB2008 can fail during geomagnetic storms. To evaluate whether AI can better capture this transient behavior, the 2025 MIT ARCLab Prize for AI Innovation in Space asked participants to forecast orbit-averaged density three days ahead. The training set included 8,118 samples, each with initial orbital parameters, 60 days of contextual space weather indicators, GOES X-ray flux, OMNI2 solar wind observations, and the corresponding three-day density target, plus 4,589 hidden samples reserved for private testing. Submissions were ranked on Codabench using the Orbital Density Root Mean Square Error (OD-RMSE), a custom metric that emphasizes early-horizon performance and is benchmarked against MSIS. The competition attracted 139 teams and 973 submissions. The development kit with the baseline solutions, evaluation scripts, the challenge documentation, and the description of the dataset is provided in STORM-AI Devkit GitHub. More details on the challenge dataset, design, and results can be found in the related publications.

candidates.title: Data from: The Salmonella In Silico Typing Resource (SISTR): an open web-accessible tool for rapidly typing and subtyping draft Salmonella genome assemblies
candidates.description: For nearly 100 years serotyping has been the gold standard for the identification of Salmonella serovars. Despite the increasing adoption of DNA-based subtyping approaches, serotype information remains a cornerstone in food safety and public health activities aimed at reducing the burden of salmonellosis. At the same time, recent advances in whole-genome sequencing (WGS) promise to revolutionize our ability to perform advanced pathogen characterization in support of improved source attribution and outbreak analysis. We present the Salmonella In Silico Typing Resource (SISTR), a bioinformatics platform for rapidly performing simultaneous in silico analyses for several leading subtyping methods on draft Salmonella genome assemblies. In addition to performing serovar prediction by genoserotyping, this resource integrates sequence-based typing analyses for: Multi-Locus Sequence Typing (MLST), ribosomal MLST (rMLST), and core genome MLST (cgMLST). We show how phylogenetic context from cgMLST analysis can supplement the genoserotyping analysis and increase the accuracy of in silico serovar prediction to over 94.6% on a dataset comprised of 4,188 finished genomes and WGS draft assemblies. In addition to allowing analysis of user-uploaded whole-genome assemblies, the SISTR platform incorporates a database comprising over 4,000 publicly available genomes, allowing users to place their isolates in a broader phylogenetic and epidemiological context. The resource incorporates several metadata driven visualizations to examine the phylogenetic, geospatial and temporal distribution of genome-sequenced isolates. As sequencing of Salmonella isolates at public health laboratories around the world becomes increasingly common, rapid in silico analysis of minimally processed draft genome assemblies provides a powerful approach for molecular epidemiology in support of public health investigations. Moreover, this type of integrated analysis using multiple sequence-based methods of sub-typing allows for continuity with historical serotyping data as we transition towards the increasing adoption of genomic analyses in epidemiology. The SISTR platform is freely available on the web at https://lfz.corefacility.ca/sistr-app/.

candidates.title: Transcriptional patterns of sexual dimorphism and in host developmental programs in the model parasitic nematode Heligmosomoides bakeri
candidates.description: Background Heligmosomoides bakeri (often mistaken for Heligmosomoides polygyrus ) is a promising model for parasitic nematodes with the key advantage of being amenable to study and manipulation within a controlled laboratory environment. While draft genome sequences are available for this worm, which allow for comparative genomic analyses between nematodes, there is a notable lack of information on its gene expression. Methods We generated biologically replicated RNA-seq datasets from samples taken throughout the parasitic life of H. bakeri . RNA from tissue-dwelling and lumen-dwelling worms, collected under a dissection microscope, was sequenced on an Illumina platform. Results We find extensive transcriptional sexual dimorphism throughout the fourth larval and adult stages of this parasite and identify alternative splicing, glycosylation, and ubiquitination as particularly important processes for establishing and/or maintaining sex-specific gene expression in this species. We find sex-linked differences in transcription related to aging and oxidative and osmotic stress responses. We observe a starvation-like signature among transcripts whose expression is consistently upregulated in males, which may reflect a higher energy expenditure by male worms. We detect evidence of increased importance for anaerobic respiration among the adult worms, which coincides with the parasite’s migration into the physiologically hypoxic environment of the intestinal lumen. Furthermore, we hypothesize that oxygen concentration may be an important driver of the worms encysting in the intestinal mucosa as larvae, which not only fully exposes the worms to their host’s immune system but also shapes many of the interactions between the host and parasite. We find stage- and sex-specific variation in the expression of immunomodulatory genes and in anthelmintic targets. Conclusions We examine how different the male and female worms are at the molecular level and describe major developmental events that occur in the worm, which extend our understanding of the interactions between this parasite and its host. In addition to generating new hypotheses for follow-up experiments into the worm’s behavior, physiology, and metabolism, our datasets enable future more in-depth comparisons between nematodes to better define the utility of H. bakeri as a model for parasitic nematodes in general.

candidates.title: Data and code from: Using phylogenetic network methods for genomic data exploration and hypothesis generation fails to untangle a confusing history of hybridization in New Zealand cicadas
candidates.description: Rapid species radiations make hybridization among species more likely. Detecting and reconstructing hybridization is, therefore, critical for understanding species relationships in many cases. We explored the relative performance of two phylogenetic network methods, SNaQ, a gene tree-based method, and PhyNEST, a site pattern-based method, in evaluating the plausibility of proposed past hybridization hypotheses. As our study system, we used the New Zealand cicada genera Kikihia and Maoricicada . Previous phylogenomic work on these two species' radiations suggested multiple hybridization events. We generated hypotheses for specific hybridization events based on observed hybrid mating songs and patterns of mito-nuclear discordance. We inferred phylogenetic networks using SNaQ and PhyNEST and a phylogenomic dataset of over 500 nuclear Anchored Hybrid Enrichment genes along with mitochondrial genomes to determine whether the two methods recovered plausible networks with respect to our hypothesized hybridization events. We also examined how the D-statistic performed in identifying our predicted hybridization events. We found that both SNaQ and PhyNEST, along with the D-statistic, recovered an extensive history of reticulate evolution in New Zealand cicadas which broadly matched our predictions. We found differences between networks inferred by the two network programs that may reflect differences in the inference methods or result from using site patterns versus gene trees as input data. Finally, we discuss considerations for users applying these methods to targeted enrichment data and suggest improvements for network method developers.

candidates.description: Code and recorded filter outputs that regenerate every table, figure and in-text number of the paper You Should Be Properly Scoring Your Odometry. The paper scores the position uncertainty that odometry systems report. Its case study covers four LiDAR-inertial filters (Fast-LIO2, Faster-LIO, Point-LIO, I2EKF-LO), the GLIM smoother and the KISS-ICP baseline on 12 Oxford Spires and 55 GEODE tracks. The package does not rerun the filters. It starts from their recorded outputs and reproduces the results on a CPU in about a quarter of an hour. - pso-code.tar.gz: the analysis scripts, the frozen outputs they are checked against, and a README with the steps. - pso-runs.tar.zst: the recorded belief tracks and provenance of the 724 filter runs the paper uses. - pso-caches.tar.zst: intermediate per-pose and per-scan results, so the paper's numbers can be regenerated without the ground truth. The ground truth is not included; but available in the public datasets, and the package pins the files it used by checksum. Scoring uses smfeval(github.com/svendbot/smfeval), which the setup step fetches at the commit the paper used.

candidates.description: This dataset provides the supporting case-level data for the manuscript “Engineering-Geological Architecture Governs Inherited-State Evolution and Reactivation-Threshold Erosion of Loess Landslides under Successive Earthquakes.” The dataset contains the case-level registry and associated numerical outputs from 528 successive-earthquake simulations representing three contrasting engineering-geological endmembers (A, B, and C). The archived files document the simulation-case structure, prescribed resistance-state protocol, principal loading and state variables, response classifications, A/B reactivation-threshold brackets, data-field definitions, and file-integrity checks. The dataset supports the analyses of inherited mechanical-state evolution, architecture-conditioned reactivation resistance, mechanically distinct State 0/1/2 response pathways, and cross-architecture transfer presented in the manuscript and Supplementary Material. A data dictionary and dataset-structure file are included to facilitate interpretation and reuse.

candidates.title: Geometry and measured intonation of 62 historical nays (1718-1936): digitised corpus
candidates.description: Digitised corpus of 62 historical nays held in Turkish museum and private collections, supporting a research article currently under review. For each instrument the file gives the collection and accession number, the total length, the outer and inner tube diameters, the measured position of each of the seven finger holes with the position prescribed by the classical 26-unit rule and the deviation between them, and, for the 34 instruments that were in a condition to be played, the seven adjacent intervals of the measured rast scale in Holder commas. Making dates are given for the 17 instruments where the source records a defensible one. The measurements were made by A. Tan between 2009 and 2011 with access granted by the holding institutions, and were published in his doctoral thesis (Marmara University, 2012) in Turkish. This deposit transcribes those tables into machine-readable form and documents them in English for the first time. The Topkapı inner diameters and a few finger-hole diameters, recorded in the same fieldwork but not printed in the thesis, are taken from A. Tan's measurement records, against which the digitised values were also cross-checked. The deposit contains no new measurement. See README.md for the column reference, the sign convention of the deviation columns, and the limitations of the dataset. The analysis code that reproduces every number and figure in the article is included as nay_analysis_code.zip.

candidates.title: Latent Human Rights Scores Version 2
candidates.description: The latent Human Rights Protection Scores (version 2) available in this section were generated using a dynamic ordinal item-response theory model discussed at length in the two papers listed below. The newest version of this model is also dynamic in the treatment of the item-difficulty cut-points of the latent variable model (labeled the Dynamic Standard Model). This parameterization allows the model to account for systematic changes to the human rights country reports published annually by the US Department of State and Amnesty International. These documents are used to code standards based human rights variables by several different coding projects. According to these indicators, human rights practices have not improved over the past 35 years, despite the spread of human rights norms, better monitoring, and the increasing prevalence of electoral democracy. This empirical pattern is not an indication of stagnating human rights practices. Instead, it reflects a systematic change in the way monitors, like Amnesty International and the US State Department, encounter and interpret information about abuses. The new latent Human Rights Protection Scores (version 2) demonstrate that respect for human rights has improved over time. Information about the earlier version of this model and data are available in the version 1 sections below. The JAGS code used to estimate the models are avai lable in the Appendix section of the article.

candidates.title: Voxel-level recovery of the oxygen-transfer constant from exported DSC-MRI capillary-function maps (results and analysis code)
candidates.description: Derivative numerical data and analysis code accompanying *Model-based oxygen extraction capacity from capillary-function DSC-MRI: voxelwise verification and parameter sensitivity* (Öchsner, Liebig, Forbrig, Reis). The study examined native-grid DSC-MRI transit-time and model-based oxygen-extraction maps from 122 adults with untreated IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, processed using Cercare Medical Neurosuite v16.2 (release-2023-02-01-03). It recovered the implemented model constant, verified the exported values within storage precision under a specified rounding assumption, and assessed how changing the constant affects absolute values, normal-appearing white-matter-normalised measurements, rankings and tumour-compartment contrasts. The alternative constant is illustrative, not a physiological recalibration. The deposit contains non-spatial derivative tables and numerical summaries, source-linked reported results, analysis code, unit tests and independent cross-checks. A public script reproduces 22 selected numerical checks from these data. The source-image extraction script `extract_voxels_export_grid.py` is provided as a separate file for the same record (SHA-256 `b71a80399200527463850e346c4a0a8689769992fc94a368d4dc5b7a0221009b`); verify it appears on the Zenodo draft before publishing. The script produces restricted spatial voxel tables; those tables are not public. Spatial voxel-level data capable of reconstructing patient images are not publicly available under the institutional ethics approval. Public participant keys are linked to the companion feature dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.21908596). This deposit does not establish physiological validity of OEFmax.

candidates.title: Data from: Secure and secret cooperation in robot swarms
candidates.description: The importance of swarm robotics systems in both academic research and real-world applications is steadily increasing. However, to reach widespread adoption, new models that ensure the secure cooperation of large groups of robots need to be developed. This work introduces a method to encapsulate cooperative robotic missions in an authenticated data structure known as Merkle tree. With this method, operators can provide the "blueprint" of the swarm's mission without disclosing its raw data. In other words, data verification can be separated from data itself. We propose a system where robots in a swarm, to cooperate towards mission completion, have to "prove'' their integrity to their peers by exchanging cryptographic proofs. We show the implications of this approach for two different swarm robotics missions: foraging and maze formation. In both missions, swarm robots were able to cooperate and carry out sequential tasks without having explicit knowledge about the mission's high-level objectives. The results presented in this work demonstrate the feasibility of using Merkle trees as a cooperation mechanism for swarm robotics systems in both simulation and real-robot experiments, which has implications for future decentralized robotics applications where security plays a crucial role. This dataset includes all experimental data generated for this paper.

The license and terms of reuse are shown in the following chapter below. -------------------------------------------------------------------- LICENSE -------------------------------------------------------------------- ______ReadMe file license______ ReadMe by Kateřina Skleničková is licensed under CC BY 4.0 License information: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ ______Dataset license______ Dataset for Insights on natural degradation in fully aliphatic biodegradable polyurethane foams by Kateřina Skleničková, Sabina Abbrent, Olga Kočková, Andrii Mahun, Libor Kobera, Václav Pokorný, Jiří Hodan, Gabriela Santos Medeiros, Nafisa Bala, Eugene Oga, Alena Kubátová, Hynek Beneš is licensed under CC BY 4.0 License information: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ -------------------------------------------------------------------- DESCRIPTION AND METHODOLOGY -------------------------------------------------------------------- ______About the dataset______ A detailed description of the methodology is provided in the main manuscript. PUR-0years - fresh PUR foam without natural aging, PUR-2years - PUR foam for 2 years naturally aged, PUR-4years - PUR foam for 4 years naturally aged, PUR-8years - PUR foam for 8 years naturally aged ______Sample preparation______ Fully aliphatic biodegradable PUR (Al-PUR) foams were prepared from poly[(diethylenglycol)adipate] diol (synthesized via polycondensation as described before having a hydroxyl number of 35 mg KOH g-1), silicone surfactant (Niax™ L-6900, Momentive), gelling catalyst, dibutyltin dilaurate (DBTL, Sigma Aldrich), blowing catalyst N,N,N',N'',N''-pentamethyldiethylenetriamine (Polycat™ 9, Air Products) and trimer of hexamethylene diisocyanate (t-HDI, Desmodur™ N 3300, with an isocyanate content of 5.2 mmol·g-1). The detailed preparation and composition of Al-PUR foams are described in our previous studies and the formulation is shown in Table A1. The only difference in the fully Al-PUR foam materials tested in this study is the year of preparation; 0-years old (freshly prepared), 1-year old, 2-years old, 4-years old and 8-years old Al-PUR foams were used. All Al-PUR foams were stored in the dark at room temperature (20–22 °C) with 10–30% relative humidity. ______Methods of data collection______ Apparent density of the prepared Al-PUR foams was determined according to ISO 845. Attenuated total reflectance–Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) Spectra of the prepared Al-PUR foams were recorded on a Spectrum 100 instrument (PerkinElmer, US) equipped with the Hg−Cd−Te detector and a universal ATR accessory with a diamond prism. Four scans per spectrum (650–4000 cm-1) at the resolution 4 cm-1 were obtained. Water vapor sorption measurements were performed using a gravimetric sorption analyzer (IGA-002, Hiden Isochema, UK). Prior to analysis, all samples (40–60 mg) were degassed under high vacuum (p ≤ 10-6 mbar) at 30 °C for a minimum of 2 h, with all tubing and chambers simultaneously decontaminated under vacuum. After degassing, the samples were stabilized at 25 °C, where sorption–desorption isotherms were collected. The measurements were carried out by stepwise increases of water vapor pressure in the range of 0–25 mbar, at a ramp rate of 2 mbar/min. At each stage of the process, the sample was stabilized, and buoyancy corrections were applied automatically by the instrument software. Relative humidity (RH) values were calculated as RH (%) = P·100 / P0, where P is the applied water vapor pressure and P0 is the saturation vapor pressure of water at 25 °C. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) Images of PUR foams were acquired on a Vega Plus TS 5135 (Tescan, CZ). This electron microscope uses secondary electron imaging (SEM/SE) at 30 kV. Al-PUR foam samples were cut in liquid nitrogen, fixed on a metallic support with conductive carbon adhesive tape, and dried in the vacuum dryer at 40 °C. Moistless foams were sputtered with platinum for 120 s (vacuum sputter coater, SCD 050, Balzers, LIE). The captured images (in perpendicular direction to the foam rise) were analyzed to determine the average cell size using ImageJ 1.54f software using a manual counting of 150 cells. Gel content, i.e. insoluble (crosslinked) fraction of Al-PUR foams, was determined using the extraction in acetone. The foam sample was weighed (morig) and then immersed in acetone and shaken for 24 hours at room temperature. Then, the sample was filtered, and the solid residues were dried at 80 °C in vacuum to constant weight (mdry). The gel content (wt%) was determined as the mdry·100 / morig. Each sample was tested in triplicate. Wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) The structure of a series of naturally aged Al-PUR foams was investigated using WAXS (Wide-angle X-ray scattering). The experiments were performed using a pinhole camera (modified molecular metrology system; Rigaku, JAP) attached to a microfocused X-ray beam generator (Rigaku MicroMax 003) operated at 50 kV and 0.6 mA (30 W). The camera was equipped with a vacuum compatible version of Pilatus3 R 300 K hybrid photon-counting detector. The sample-to-detector distance (calibrated using a silicon powder sample) was 52 mm and the exposure time used was 4 hours. Tensile tests The mechanical properties of ten dumbbell-shaped specimens were measured at room temperature using test method ISO 1798. The cross-head speed was set to 500 mm/min and a load cell was set at 100 N being measured by Instron model 6025/5800R (Instron Limited, High Wycombe, UK). Each specimen had a total length of 115 mm, a width of 6 mm in the middle part, and a width of 25 mm in the end part (according to ISO 1798/1A). Dynamic-mechanical and thermal analysis (DMTA) Dynamic-mechanical properties of the Al-PUR foams were measured on an ARES-G2 rheometer (TA Instruments, US) using rectangular samples (30×10×5 mm). Dynamic oscillatory shear measurements were performed in a temperature range of -80–150 °C using a temperature ramp of 3 °C min−1, 0.5 % strain and 1 Hz frequency. The temperature dependence of the storage (G') and loss (G'') shear moduli and loss factor (tan δ) were evaluated. The main (α) transition temperature (Tα) was determined as the maximum of the tan δ curve (with precision of Tα ± 2 °C). A deconvolution of the tan δ curves (plotted on a linear scale) was performed using Fityk software (version 1.3.1). Gaussian functions were employed to model the phases in polymer structures. The relative peak areas were used to estimate the proportion of each phase within Al-PUR structure. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) TGA of Al-PUR foams was performed on a Pyris 1 TGA (PerkinElmer, US). The sample of ca. 2 mg was heated from room temperature to 750 °C with a heating rate of 10 °C·min-1 under inert gas (nitrogen) flow of 25 cm3·min-1. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) DSC was conducted using a 2000 calorimeter from TA Instruments (US) to examine the thermal characteristics of Al-PUR samples. The measurements involved multiple heating-cooling-heating cycles spanning from -100 °C to 250 °C, with a heating rate of 10 °C min-1, and a nitrogen purge of 50 mL min-1. The glass transition temperature (Tg) was identified based on the second heating cycle. Evolved gas analysis-mass spectrometry (EGA-MS) and thermal desorption-pyrolysis-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (TD-Py-GC-MS) All experiments utilized a PY-3030D multi-shot pyrolyzer with an autosampler (Frontier Laboratories, Japan) coupled to an Agilent 7890A GC with 5975C MS system (Agilent Technologies, USA). The analyses were performed in two modes. First, experiments were conducted using EGA-MS, in which the GC column was replaced by a deactivated tube (Ultra ALLOY-DTM, 0.15 mm I.D. × 2.5 m length, Frontier Laboratories, Japan) to enable a direct analyte transfer from the pyrolyzer to MS. The pyrolyzer temperature program started at 90 °C, was held for 0.2 min, and proceeded with a 20 °C/min gradient up to 800 °C, which was held for 1 min. Evolved gases from the sample were transferred directly to the MSD with helium as a carrier gas at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min. The GC inlet was operated in a split mode (1:20) with the temperature set at 300 °C. The MS analysis was performed without the solvent delay using an electron ionization (EI) source at 70 eV in a mass range of 10–700 m/z with a scan rate of 7.1 seconds/per scan. The second mode of analysis, TD-Py-GC–MS, utilized an Agilent J&W DB-5 MS capillary column (30 m length, 0.25 mm internal diameter, and 0.25 μm film thickness). The TD-Py program (designed based on the results obtained from EGA-MS, see Figure A1) enabled a sequential thermal treatment of samples with six temperature steps at 20 °C/min gradient: 90–250 °C, 250–310 °C, 310–360 °C, 360–420 °C, 420–550 °C, 550–710 °C each followed by GC analysis. The GC inlet temperature was held at 300 °C operated in split mode (1:20). The flow rate of helium was 1.0 mL·min-1. The GC oven temperature program started with cryogenic trapping with liquid nitrogen at the front of the column during the pyrolyzer heating steps, followed by a column temperature starting at 40 °C held for 1 min, and a gradient of 25 °C/min up to 320 °C, held for 4 min. The MS analysis was performed without solvent delay with EI at 70 eV, a mass range of 10–700 m/z with a scan rate of 2.66 scans/s. Solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR) Spectra were recorded at 16.4 T using a Bruker AVANCE NEO spectrometer. The 3.2-mm cross-polarization magic-angle spinning (CP/MAS) probe was used for 13C ss NMR experiments at Larmor frequency of ν(13C) =176.048 MHz. 13C NMR chemical shift was calibrated using α-glycine (176.03 ppm; carbonyl signal) as an external standard. The 13C MAS spectra were acquired at the speed of the sample spinning of 15 kHz with 20 s recycle delay and 1024–2560 number of scans. All ss NMR experiments were conducted under active cooling in order to compensate for frictional heating caused by the rotation of the samples. All experiments were done at 298 K temperature. Approximately 1 mg of a ground sample was deposited on the ground-steel target plate, pressed with a spatula, overlaid by 1 µL matrix solution (2,5-dihydroxybenzoic acid; Sigma–Aldrich, 98 % in DMF; 20 mg mL-1) and dried under ambient conditions. The spectra were recorded as the sum of 25,000 shots with a DPSS Nd: YAG laser (355 nm, 2,000 Hz). External calibration was used for molecular weight assignment. ______Methods of data processing______ The dataset contains only raw data from the main paper; therefore, no processing is described. The detailed preparation and composition of Al-PUR foams are described in our previous studies and the formulation is shown in Table A1. The only difference in the fully Al-PUR foam materials tested in this study is the year of preparation; 0-years old (freshly prepared), 1-year old, 2-years old, 4-years old and 8-years old Al-PUR foams were used. Prior to analysis, all samples (40–60 mg) were degassed under high vacuum (p ≤ 10-6 mbar) at 30 °C for a minimum of 2 h, with all tubing and chambers simultaneously decontaminated under vacuum. The measurements were carried out by stepwise increases of water vapor pressure in the range of 0–25 mbar, at a ramp rate of 2 mbar/min. At each stage of the process, the sample was stabilized, and buoyancy corrections were applied automatically by the instrument software. candidates.title: Maize tassel detection from UAV imagery using deep learning
candidates.description: Dataset associated with paper titled "Maize Tassel Detection from UAV Imagery Using Deep Learning" published on the journal of Frontiers in Robotics and AI (DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2021.600410). The timing of flowering plays a critical role in determining the productivity of agricultural crops. If the crops flower too early, the crop would mature before the end of the growing season, losing the opportunity to capture and use large amounts of light energy. If the crops flower too late, the crop may be killed by the change of seasons before it is ready to harvest. Maize flowering is one of the most important periods where even small amounts of stress can significantly alter yield. In this work, we developed and compared two methods for automatic tassel detection based on the imagery collected from an unmanned aerial vehicle, using deep learning models. The first approach was a customized framework for tassel detection based on convolutional neural network (TD-CNN). The other method was a state-of-the-art object detection technique of the faster region-based CNN (Faster R-CNN), serving as baseline detection accuracy. The evaluation criteria for tassel detection were customized to correctly reflect the needs of tassel detection in an agricultural setting. Although detecting thin tassels in the aerial imagery is challenging, our results showed promising accuracy: the TD-CNN had an F1 score of 95.9% and the Faster R-CNN had 97.9% F1 score. More CNN-based model structures can be investigated in the future for improved accuracy, speed, and generalizability on aerial-based tassel detection. The dataset including raw images and labelled images are here. The code are available on Dr. Aziza Alzadjali's GitHub account "azizanajeeb" (github.com).

candidates.title: Thai SDG-labelled Text Corpus (v1.2)
candidates.description: Thai SDG-labelled Text Corpus (v1.2) The Thai SDG-labelled Text Corpus is a publicly available dataset for Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) text classification in Thai. The corpus contains 6,800 records evenly balanced across all 17 SDGs (400 records per goal). It was derived from the OSDG Community Dataset (OSDG-CD), Version 2024.04 (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11441197), translated into Thai using machine translation, with additional expert review of records flagged by automatic quality-control checks, and augmented with expert-reviewed synthetic data for SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), which is not included in the original OSDG-CD. The dataset is intended to support Thai-language and multilingual natural language processing (NLP) research, including SDG classification, cross-lingual learning, information retrieval, and policy document analysis. Version 1.1 update Version 1.1 : Updated the dataset documentation and metadata to correct the author surname and update the source OSDG-CD citation to Version 2024.04 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11441197). Corrected the description of expert_agreement_score and the reporting of inter-annotator agreement. The field represents raw percent (observed) agreement and is not Cohen's kappa. candidates.title: Data-Matrix Permeability Regulates the Hydraulic and Mechanical Influence of the Natural Fracture Network, in Matrix Permeability Regulates the Hydraulic and Mechanical Influence of the Natural Fracture Network
candidates.description: This project investigates the coupled hydraulic and mechanical response of naturally fractured sandstone formations during supercritical carbon dioxide (CO₂) injection for geological carbon storage. The primary objective is to understand how rock matrix permeability and pre-existing natural fractures influence fluid pressure buildup, pressure diffusion, fluid storage, deformation, and stress redistribution within geological formations. The study uses the coupled finite–discrete element method (FDEM) to simulate CO₂ injection into homogeneous and naturally fractured Dakota and Entrada sandstone formations in the Uinta Basin, Utah. These formations have different hydraulic and mechanical properties, allowing comparisons of their responses under similar injection conditions. The numerical models incorporate in-situ stresses, matrix permeability, rock mechanical properties, and natural fracture networks. The simulations examine wellbore pressure evolution, fluid diffusion patterns, volumetric deformation, pressure-related and strain-related fluid storage, and local shear stress mobilization. Particular attention is given to understanding how natural fractures provide preferential fluid flow pathways and influence mechanical interactions between rock blocks. The uniqueness of this project lies in evaluating the combined effects of matrix permeability and natural fractures on injection-induced hydromechanical behavior. The dataset can be reused to compare reservoir responses, investigate fluid transport mechanisms, validate numerical modeling approaches, and support future studies of injection-induced geomechanical instability. The intended audience includes researchers and engineers working in rock mechanics, geotechnical engineering, reservoir engineering, computational geomechanics, and geological CO₂ storage.

candidates.title: Draft Papilio alphenor assembly and annotation
candidates.description: Novel phenotypes are increasingly recognized to have evolved by co-option of conserved genes into new developmental contexts, yet the process by which co-opted genes modify existing developmental programs remains obscure. Here we provide insight into this process by characterizing the role of co-opted doublesex in butterfly wing color pattern development. dsx is the master regulator of insect sex differentiation but was co-opted to control the switch between discrete non-mimetic and mimetic patterns in Papilio alphenor and its relatives. We found dynamic spatial and temporal expression pattern differences between mimetic and non-mimetic butterflies throughout wing development. A mimetic color pattern program is switched on by a pulse of dsx expression in early pupal development that causes acute and long-term differential gene expression, particularly in Wnt and Hedgehog signaling pathways. RNAi suggested opposing, novel roles for these pathways in mimetic pattern development. Importantly, Dsx co-option caused Engrailed, a key transcription factor target of Hedgehog signaling, to gain a novel expression domain early in pupal wing development that is propagated through mid-pupal development to specify novel mimetic patterns despite becoming decoupled from Dsx expression itself. Altogether, our findings provide multiple views into how co-opted genes can both cause and elicit changes to conserved networks and pathways to result in development of novel, adaptive phenotypes. This dataset contains the genome assembly and annotation described in the associated manuscript. Sequencing data, including all RNA-seq data, is available under the NCBI under BioProject PRJNA882073.

candidates.title: Data from: Quantifying and linking mechanism scenarios to invasive species impact
candidates.description: Plant species invasion represents one of the major drivers of biodiversity change globally, yet there is confusion about the nature of non-indigenous species (NIS) impact. This stems from differing notions of what constitutes invasive species impact and the scales at which it should be assessed. At local scales, the mechanisms of impact on local competitors can be classified into four scenarios: 1) minimal impact from NIS inhabiting unique niches; 2) neutral impact spread across the community and proportional to NIS abundance; 3) targeted impact on a small number of competitors with overlapping niches; and 4) pervasive impact that is disproportionate to NIS abundance and caused by modifications that filter out other species. I developed a statistical test to distinguish these four mechanism scenarios based on plant community rank-abundance curves and then created a scale-independent standardized impact score. Using an example long-term dataset, that has high native plant diversity and an abundance gradient of the invasive vine, Vincetoxicum rossicum , I show that impact resulted in either targeted or pervasive extirpations. Regardless of whether NIS impact is neutral, targeted, or pervasive, the net outcome will be the homogenization of ecosystems and reduced biodiversity at larger scales, perhaps reducing ecosystem resilience. The framework and statistical evaluation of impact presented in this paper provide researchers and managers with an objective approach to quantifying NIS impact and prioritizing species for further management actions.

candidates.title: Naija Audio Data
candidates.description: The Naija Audio Transcription Dataset comprises five WAV audio items accompanied by transcription and annotation data in JSON format. The JSON file, Trancribed Naija Audio Data.json, contains the full transcription associated with each audio item, language and acoustic labels, annotator notes where available, and annotation metadata. The transcription text is written in Latin script as supplied in the dataset. All five records contain a full-transcription field, a language selection recorded as Other (note in comment), and an acoustic label of Mobile — minor noise. Four records include notes stating that the language is Naija and that the original data provided was translated into Naija because data in Naija was not available. The JSON documents this translation-related step but does not fully specify the original source material or the process used to create the audio. Two of the five records contain time-aligned annotations, including segment start and end times, channel information, speech labels, and associated text linked to particular intervals. However, time-aligned annotations are not available for every audio item, and segment and text entries are not consistently paired throughout the JSON. Users requiring complete word-level or time-aligned transcriptions should review the annotations before using the dataset for such purposes. The JSON also contains task identifiers, annotation identifiers, timestamps, and other annotation-tool metadata. One record includes a draft transcription that represents the year in words, while the saved transcription uses numerals. The saved transcription is the primary recorded annotation; the status of the draft should be confirmed against the project’s annotation workflow where relevant. The dataset may be useful for linguistic research involving Naija transcription and for developing or testing speech and language processing workflows. Its suitability for specific applications should be assessed in light of the partial time-aligned annotations and the provenance and methodological information not documented in the JSON.

candidates.title: NITROSAMINES AND NITROSAMINE DRUG SUBSTANCE-RELATED IMPURITIES (NDSRIs) IN PHARMACEUTICAL PREPARATIONS: FORMATION MECHANISMS, ANALYTICAL DETECTION, AND TOXICOLOGICAL RISK ASSESSMENT
candidates.description: Nitrosamines and nitrosamine drug substance-related impurities (NDSRIs) have emerged as important pharmaceutical contaminants because of their potential genotoxic and carcinogenic effects, even at very low exposure levels. Their formation may occur during active pharmaceutical ingredient synthesis, drug product manufacturing, storage, or through interactions between amine-containing drug substances and nitrosating agents such as nitrites. The structural diversity of NDSRIs and their occurrence at trace concentrations present significant challenges for pharmaceutical quality control and toxicological risk assessment. Modern analytical technologies, particularly liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS), and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), provide sensitive and selective approaches for the detection, identification, and quantification of nitrosamine impurities. In parallel, toxicological assessment based on structure–activity relationships, read-across approaches, computational toxicology, and the principles described in ICH M7 has become increasingly important for establishing acceptable intake limits. An integrated strategy combining risk assessment, sensitive analytical methods, process control, and toxicological evaluation is therefore essential for effective management of nitrosamine-related risks in pharmaceutical products. Continued development of high-resolution analytical technologies and predictive toxicology is expected to improve the early identification and prevention of potentially hazardous nitrosamine impurities .

candidates.title: Optical maps refine the bread wheat Triticum aestivum cv Chinese Spring genome assembly
candidates.description: This dataset contains a single whole-genome optical map file (.CMAP) for bread wheat ( Triticum aestivum ) cv Chinese Spring (CS). The methods for constructing this optical map and the properties of this map are described below. The definition of the CMAP format is documented in https://bionanogenomics.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/30039-CMAP-File-Format-Specification-Sheet.pdf. The extracted ultra-high-molecular weight DNA molecules of CS were labeled with the DLE-1 enzyme (Bionano Genomics, San Diego, CA, USA) and were then stained with the Bionano PrepTM DLS Kit (Bionano Genomics, San Diego, CA, USA). A consensus optical map was de novo assembled with the Assembler tool of the Bionano Solve v3.3 package using significance cutoffs of P < 1 × 10 -11 to generate draft consensus contigs, P < 1 × 10 -12 for draft consensus contig extension, and P < 1 × 10 -16 for final merging of the draft consensus contigs. A recipe of “nonhaplotype”, “noES”, and “noCut” was chosen. The initial optical map was then checked for potential chimeric contigs. Images of DLE-1-labeled CS DNA molecules > 150 kb and equivalent to about 136x genome coverage were collected and assembled into a whole-genome optical map. The map contained 726 contigs with an N50 of 55.01 Mb and a total length of 14.41 Gb.

candidates.title: A high-quality genome assembly and annotation of the gray mangrove, Avicennia marina
candidates.description: The gray mangrove [ Avicennia marina (Forsk.) Vierh.] is the most widely distributed mangrove species, ranging throughout the Indo-West Pacific. It presents remarkable levels of geographic variation both in phenotypic traits and habitat, often occupying extreme environments at the edges of its distribution. However, subspecific evolutionary relationships and adaptive mechanisms remain understudied, especially across populations of the West Indian Ocean. High-quality genomic resources accounting for such variability are also sparse. Here we report the first chromosome-level assembly of the genome of A. marina . We used a previously release draft assembly and proximity ligation libraries Chicago and Dovetail HiC for scaffolding, producing a 456,526,188 bp long genome. The largest 32 scaffolds (22.4 Mb to 10.5 Mb) accounted for 98 % of the genome assembly, with the remaining 2% distributed among much shorter 3,759 scaffolds (62.4 Kb to 1 Kb). We annotated 45,032 protein-coding genes using tissue-specific RNA-seq data in combination with de novo gene prediction, from which 34,442 were associated to GO terms. Genome assembly and annotated set of genes yield a 96.7% and 95.1% completeness score, respectively, when compared with the eudicots BUSCO dataset. Furthermore, an F ST survey based on resequencing data successfully identified a set of candidate genes potentially involved in local adaptation, and revealed patterns of adaptive variability correlating with a temperature gradient in Arabian mangrove populations. Our A. marina genomic assembly provides a highly valuable resource for genome evolution analysis, as well as for identifying functional genes involved in adaptive processes and speciation.

candidates.title: Data and code for: Learned quadrotor force models under flight-regime shift: calibrated uncertainty, miss runs and online recalibration with delayed force feedback
candidates.description: Supporting data and analysis code for the article Learned quadrotor force models under flight-regime shift: calibrated uncertainty, miss runs and online recalibration with delayed force feedback by S. Sahay, H. Yadav, A. Jaiswal and R. Tiwari (Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai). The study trains a fitted physics model and hybrid physics + LightGBM and physics + MLP-ensemble force models on the 95 real flights of the public NeuroBEM quadrotor dataset, calibrates them by split conformal prediction under five train/test protocols (held-out flights, official split, held-out manoeuvre family, speed shift, random rows), and compares offline and online (ACI, DtACI, quantile tracking) recalibration with delayed and noisy force feedback. Contents tableS2_all_methods_targets_splits.csv : every result, one row per split, model, target, method, level, label delay and noise level (Online Resource 2, Table S2). tableS2_data_dictionary.csv : definition and unit of every column of Table S2. split_membership.csv : role of each of the 95 NeuroBEM flights in every time-ordered split. neurobem_regime_shift_code_and_results.zip : complete analysis code (Python; run_all.sh , requirements.txt ) and every derived result file behind the figures and tables. neurobem_regime_shift_online_traces.zip : per-split online interval traces (NumPy), needed only to redraw the miss-run figure. The NeuroBEM flight data (Bauersfeld et al., RSS 2021) are not redistributed; the code downloads them from the original site (https://rpg.ifi.uzh.ch/NeuroBEM.html). Data files: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT licence (LICENSE_code.txt in the package).

candidates.title: Data for: Endothelial glycocalyx disruption as a driver of blood–brain barrier dysfunction
candidates.description: This dataset contains the raw and processed quantitative data supporting the manuscript “Endothelial Glycocalyx Disruption as a Driver of Blood-Brain Barrier Dysfunction” (O’Hare et al., 2026). It combines in vivo cerebral microvascular measurements from young adult, aged, APP/PS1 Alzheimer’s disease, and mild traumatic brain injury mouse cohorts with in vitro measurements from human blood-brain barrier models following selective knockdown of the endothelial glycocalyx core proteins CD44 or syndecan-1. The deposited workbook includes quantitative measurements of glycocalyx composition, endothelial junctional organization, transporter expression, vascular inflammation, and barrier permeability. Raw, normalized, biological-replicate, and image-level values are retained where applicable, with missing values and analysis exclusions documented in the accompanying README. The dataset can support comparative studies of neurovascular dysfunction, independent statistical reanalysis, and benchmarking of vessel-segmentation and junction-fragmentation workflows.
